 Mayor and two council seats were on the ballot

 Ontario Councilmembers Daisy Macias and Alan Wapner, and former councilmember Ruben Valencia, were leading the race for mayor and the District 3 and District 2 Council seats, respectively, as of 10 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3. (Courtesy photos)
 By Joe Nelson | jnelson@scng.com PUBLISHED: November 3, 2026 at 9:05 PM PST | UPDATED: November 3, 2026 at 11:07 PM PST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Daisy Macias was leading longtime Ontario Mayor Paul Leon in early returns Tuesday, Nov. 3, as voters weighed a change in city leadership amid an FBI investigation, questions about public spending and concerns over rapid growth.
 Macias, a City Council member, led the four-candidate mayoral race with 7,332 votes, or 38.63%, compared with Leon’s 6,137 votes, or 32.34%, according to the 10 p.m. preliminary results from the San Bernardino County Registrar of Voters. Businessman Kevin Kizzee was third with 16.73%, followed by UC Riverside student Nicolo Lalama with 12.30%.
 Macias did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
 Leon, meanwhile, acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the race while expressing gratitude for his years in public office.
 “First, I want to thank the people of Ontario. Whatever the final count, it has been the honor of my life to serve this city for almost 30 years,” Leon said in a statement following the release of the 10 p.m. preliminary results.
 Despite trailing Macias by 1,195 votes, Leon emphasized the outcome remained undecided.
 “This race is close, and in a close race every ballot matters. Thousands of ballots are still being counted, and the voters who cast them deserve to be heard,” he said.
 “We’ll wait patiently, respect the process, and accept the result. Ontario has always been bigger than any one election, any one person, and that won’t change.”
 In City Council races, former Councilmember Ruben Valencia was leading Stephanie Martinez in District 2 with 57.69% of the vote to Martinez’s 42.26%. Valencia had 2,235 votes to Martinez’s 1,637, a margin of 598 votes.
 “I feel good. I feel that we’re in a good spot, and hopefully everything trends in the right direction,” Valencia said Tuesday. “I had an amazing team behind me.”
 Valencia, who served on the City Council from 2016 to 2024, said he spent the past two years enjoying retirement before deciding to seek a return to city politics. He said he knocked on 4,000 doors during his campaign and heard widespread concerns about alleged corruption at City Hall.
 In District 3, longtime incumbent Councilmember Alan Wapner held a narrow lead over software engineer Michael Rios, with 2,006 votes, or 31.15%, to Rios’ 1,876 votes, or 29.13% — a margin of just 130 votes.
 Nurse and military veteran Larry Trinidad was third with 22.98%, followed by sheriff’s deputy and Planning Commissioner D’Andre Lampkin with 16.73%.
 Wapner declined to comment Tuesday, saying too few precincts had reported results to assess the outcome of the race.
 The election unfolded amid an ongoing FBI investigation involving Ontario officials, including Wapner.
 On July 28, agents searched properties associated with Wapner, San Bernardino County Supervisor Curt Hagman, attorney Frank Lizarraga and businessman James Su, while serving subpoenas at Ontario City Hall and Ontario International Airport. Wapner and Hagman were then president and vice president, respectively, of the Ontario International Airport Authority board.
 Authorities have not publicly disclosed the investigation’s focus, and no criminal charges have been publicly announced in connection with the case.
 Four candidates competed for mayor, including Leon , who joined the council in 1998 and became mayor in 2005. Leon emphasized fiscal responsibility and transparency, while challengers  Macias , Kizzee and UC Riverside student Lalama focused on government accountability, spending and development.
 Macias stressed fiscal responsibility, while Kizzee, who rebuilt his life as a businessman and community advocate after serving 22 years in federal prison for drug offenses and earning seven college degrees while incarcerated, called for a forensic audit of city spending in light of the recent federal investigation. Lalama campaigned on government transparency, reining in city spending and curbing warehouse overexpansion.
 In the wake of the FBI raids, Wapner abandoned his mayoral bid and instead sought reelection to his District 3 seat. A retired Ontario police sergeant, Wapner has served on the City Council since 1994. He subsequently relinquished his committee assignments, including the presidency of the Ontario International Airport Authority board.
 An October Southern California News Group investigation revealed Wapner charged the airport authority $184,997 for 72 trips over five years. Wapner defended the travel as necessary airport business, and the authority subsequently tightened its reimbursement policies.

 Wapner campaigned on reducing street racing, homelessness and traffic congestion.
 Rios campaigned against warehouse expansion, increased truck traffic and unnecessary tax hikes. Lampkin emphasized creating safer neighborhoods and economic growth, and Trinidad focused on affordability, homelessness, and increasing the number of first responders.
 In District 2,  Valencia , a retired sheriff’s deputy, emphasized homelessness, spending and campaign finance transparency, while Martinez , a bilingual interpreter, prioritized public safety and responsible economic growth.
